newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Xmas shopping to push up Philippine Nov inflation.
newsitem.headline: Xmas shopping to push up Philippine Nov inflation.

text.p: A surge in Christmas spending and hike in local transportation fares are expected to drive Philippine inflation to 5.7 percent in November from 4.7 in October, a Reuters poll showed on Tuesday.

The average 5.7 percent figure produced by the poll of five financial institutions completed on Tuesday showed year-on-year November inflation would be much lower than the year-ago 11.1 percent, when a rice shortage sent prices soaring.
The government, which last week forecast the figure in a range of 6.0-6.3 percent, is scheduled to announce November inflation figures on Thursday.
"We're assuming a month-on-month change of 0.75 to 1.0 percentage point," said Dennis Lapid, an economist at Vickers Ballas Securities.

Economists said their forecasts were generally lower than the government because the government assumed the half-month impact of an increase in transportation fares and a delay in the monthly adjustments in domestic oil prices.
"The full impact of the transportation hike is one percentage point. But only half of that will be reflected in November," said economist Lito Dalit of AsianBank Corp.
Effective last November 14, the government's Land Transportation Franchising & Regulatory Board raised bus fares by 14 to 33 percent.

The fare hike followed the government's rise in domestic fuel prices in three successive months due to the implementation of a new oil pricing scheme that would pave the way for full deregulation of the petroleum industry by March 1997.

On Tuesday, the Philippines' Energy Regulatory Board chairman Bayani Faylona told Reuters that prices of most petroleum products would again be raised by 50 centavos (two cents) per litre. The adjustments will be announced at a news conference at 12 noon (0400 GMT) on Tuesday, he said.
The decision to raise prices came after a month's delay when the adjustments were put on hold because of a complaint by a Congressman that they were unjustified.
"The delay in the oil price hike had effectively placed the clamour for higher wages out of the picture in the near term," said Paul Joseph Garcia, an economist of Metrobank.
Inflation currently is being driven by cost-push concerns, and not by money supply factors, the analysts said.
The Central Bank had reported that base money, a measure of domestic liquidity, slowed to a year-on-year growth of 7.6 percent in November from 13.2 percent in the previous month.
Analysts added that the peso remained stable, averaging 26.266 to the dollar in November from 26.27 in October.
For calendar 1996, economists expect an average inflation rate at 8.7 percent in line with the government's target.

The 1996 forecast is above the 1995 average of 8.1 percent due to the effect of severe rice shortages, which sent inflation to a year-high of 11.8 percent in February. Inflation tapered off to single digit in June until it bottomed out at 4.4 percent in September.
